chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
title: Les Koenig's relaxed recording sessions
summary: Johnson contrasts Contemporary Records' open-ended sessions with East Coast practice.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah, what you were saying about that, the way Nesser records reminds me of Les Koenig, because when he ran Contemporary Records, that's when I went out there, I heard Ornette's first album, then I saw some other things there, too. He would start the tape as soon as anybody came in, and just keep them going, all day, the next day, didn't care. There was a refrigerator full of beer and sandwiches and stuff like that, always replenished, and nobody said a word about time. When the musicians were tired, they stopped. That
seems to me so much the logical way to make records.
Have you heard of anybody but Nessery doing that here in the East?
Well, they take breaks at Columbia.
If they have some whisky, they bring it in. That's not the same as a guy (unintelligible) the beer.
